At Wednesday’s Quarterly Refunding Announcement, Treasury will set note and bond auction sizes for the next quarter. That starts with next week’s refunding auctions, which would total $125B if sizes are unchanged: $58B of 3s, $42B of 10s and $25B of 30s. It will also update its guidance on future coupon sales.

Some on the Street are speculating that Treasury will shift supply away from the long end, particularly 20- and 30-year bonds, and toward T-bills. Citi expects cuts to 20s and 30s starting this month. BofA, Goldman, UBS and Barclays are among those looking for a change to the “at least the next several quarters” language in place since January 2024, although UBS sees no actual change in issuance until May. JPMorgan is the notable dissent. It expects the language to hold into 2027 and argues that cutting long bonds wouldn’t be prudent given the borrowing ahead and early signs that bill demand is stalling.

The motive is yields. The 30-year was still above 5.30% on Friday after long rates hit their highest in more than two decades in early October.

That shift though would push the T-bill share of debt further above the ~20% average the TBAC advised in 2024:

▪ Bills were 22.4% of marketable debt at the end of September. Rolling that forward with daily Treasury data puts October at ~23.0%, the highest since early 2021.

▪ BofA and Goldman already see 24.3% in 2027, and Goldman 24.9% in 2028, near the 25.5% pandemic peak. That’s before any shift out of the long end.

▪ For scale, Treasury sold ~$445B of nominal 20- and 30-year bonds over the past 12 months. Moving half of that into bills would add roughly 0.7 points a year to the bill share.

Heavier bill reliance is also why gross issuance is already at a record given they need to be rolled over frequently. Treasury auctioned $839B last week, the most in data back to 1979. The 13-week average is $636B, nearly 3x the 2019 average of $226B. 

The downside of this moves to shorter maturities is that this leaves Treasury’s interest costs more exposed to swings in short-term rates, with the market pricing three more rate hikes from the Fed by the end of 2027. And while investors have piled into bills since the pandemic, there’s no assurance that demand will continue. 

Bills outstanding have nearly tripled, from $2.6T in February 2020 to $7.1T in September. JPMorgan is already flagging early signs of stalling, and the stablecoin bid Treasury officials have touted has yet to show up at scale.

Treasury also updates its quarterly borrowing estimates this afternoon.

Goldman’s Prime Book says hedge funds were starting to cover their big net short position through Thursday.  That might have been derailed by Friday's action.

They say hedge funds net bought US stocks for the first time in four weeks (October 23–29, +1.1 standard deviations vs. the past year). But it was mostly taking off their index shorts, not new longs:

▪️ Single stocks were modestly net bought after five weeks of selling, almost entirely on short covers.

▪️ The Prime data run through Thursday. Goldman’s Shares desk said hedge fund flows “finished balanced” for the full week, including Friday’s selloff.

So hedge funds were slowly taking bearish bets off, not adding risk. With net exposure still near five-year lows, there’s plenty of room for more covering, fuel for an *eventual* rally.

Looking at the seasonality breakdown from @AlmanacTrader, editor of the Stock Trader’s Almanac & Almanac Investor Newsletter (see link below), November opens with one of its strongest stretches. Hirsch counts eleven bullish days for the S&P 500 in November, including six in a row starting on the first trading day.

Monday is trading day 1. Over the past 21 years, the major indices have gained about 1–1.2% by Friday (day 5), roughly half of their full-month gain. Monday has been about flat on average, and the gains have built from Tuesday through Friday. The Russell 2000 has jumped about 0.6% on Thursday alone. The run has topped out the following Monday (day 6, Nov. 9), with the indices up about 1.2–1.5% for the month before a mid-month pullback.

And midterm years have started faster. The midterm lines are up about 0.4–0.65% after day 1. By Friday, the DJIA, S&P, Nasdaq and Russell 1000 are up about 1.7% and the Russell 2000 about 2.1%. That’s roughly half to two-thirds of their full-month gain in the first five sessions. The DJIA and S&P have done nearly all of that climbing by Wednesday, while the Nasdaq and Russells catch up on Thursday, and the run has lasted longer, to about 2% by the eighth trading day (Nov. 11). Election Day falls on Tuesday (day 2) this year. Historically, though, it has landed anywhere from the 2nd to the 6th trading day of November, so the midterm averages don’t map neatly onto a post-election reaction.

From there, Hirsch’s “strong start, mid-month dip, strong finish” pattern takes over. The indices have pulled back into trading days 13–14 (Nov. 18–19), when the 21-year averages give back most of their early gains. They then rally into month-end, finishing up about 2–2.7% across all years and 2.6–3.5% in midterm years, led by the Nasdaq.

Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson (Bloomberg Q&A Sunday) sees a few “clearing events” taking the S&P 500 to ~7,100 before a run to 8,000. The three catalysts: AI spending and capital raising, the midterms, and tighter liquidity: 

▪️ AI supply: Hyperscalers are now net issuers of equity, on top of Meta, SpaceX, the Anthropic IPO and heavy M&A issuance, plus $40 billion overnight debt deals. On Morgan Stanely's Thoughts on the Market podcast last week, he said he expects more stock and debt supply over the next few weeks and sees semis another 10% to 15% lower into mid-November. He thinks the raising cycle is late and expects a break within about 30 days.
▪️ Midterms: He calls them “always a headwind.” A Democratic House and a narrow Senate (52-48) are priced in, but a 55-45 result isn’t, and a bigger margin could fuel state and local pushback on data centers and more regulation. The larger overhang is what President Trump does after the vote, including a possible Iran escalation.
▪️ Liquidity: He called this the most important of the three on the podcast. Financial conditions are tighter, credit spreads are widening, and the government is competing for capital with no ’90s-style surplus. Quality companies can grow at today’s rates, but lower-quality small caps paying 8% to 10% to borrow can’t.

The math from Friday’s 7,580 close (−1.8%, worst day since June):
▪️ 7,100 to 7,200 = another 5% to 6.3% down (7,100 is −9.2% from the 7,818.93 record)”
▪️ 8,000 = +5.5% from here, +12.7% from 7,100

Wilson’s track record has been criticized after he was much too bearish in 2023 and 2024, but he was right in 2022, and more recently he called the March 30 low, and his 7,800 target from last November was hit October 6.

Bloomberg ran through the scenarios for the midterms this week.

Wall Street unsurprisingly is generally looking for gridlock (the call from BofA, Citi, etc.) with Citi's Stuart Kaiser calling a stymied Congress the ideal outcome with profits booming and GDP growing at a steady clip. 

History is consistent with that view. Under a Republican president with a split Congress, the S&P 500 has averaged 13.7% a year since 1950, per Carson Investment Research, versus 8.3% when Republicans controlled Congress and 4.9% when Democrats did.

A Democratic sweep, the outcome Kalshi favors, is the one most likely to spark a selloff analysts believe, mainly on the risk of AI regulation, from restrictions on data centers to rules on how models are developed. Trump's veto would make it hard to pass anything, but Democrats could still keep the pressure on the industry through investigations and hearings. 

Healthcare could benefit if they push to reverse Medicaid cuts, while defense contractors have already slumped on expectations of tighter scrutiny of military spending. 

In bonds, a blue sweep could weigh on prices if Trump, as a lame duck, leans more heavily on executive action such as new tariffs or raising geopolitical tensions, which is close to the post-midterm risk I discuss in the wrap-up. 

A Republican hold, which polls suggest is unlikely, would keep the favorable backdrop for AI stocks intact and could spark a rally in financials and industrials. As Manulife John Hancock's Matt Miskin put it, "Status quo would not be a bad thing per se."

Whatever the outcome, history is on the bulls' side. Wells Fargo found the S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months after every midterm election since World War II. 

Per Truist, stocks tend to fall in the months before a midterm and start rallying shortly before the vote (we're not seeing that second part yet). By Claude's read of Truist's chart in the piece, the average midterm year is up only about 1% at the end of October and finishes up about 5%, with roughly 3 points of that coming after Election Day (which always falls between November 2nd and 8th). 

This year, though, the S&P 500 is already up 10.7% through October.
